paragraphs.text: A DISCOURSE OF GREGORY, AMONG THE SAINTS, ON THE NATIVITY OF CHRIST AND ON THE INFANTS IN BETHLEHEM SLAIN BY HEROD. "Blow the trumpet at the new moon," says David, "on the well-marked day of your feast." The commands of divinely inspired teaching are surely law for those who hear them. Since the well-marked day of our feast is here, let us also fulfil the law and become trumpeters of the holy festival. The trumpet of the law, as the Apostle bids us understand it, is the word. For he says that the sound of the trumpet must not be indistinct, but its notes must be distinct, so that the hearers understand clearly. So let us also, brethren, sound a bright note that carries far, no less honourable than the horn trumpet. For the law too, sketching the truth in advance in the types of the shadow, prescribed the sound of trumpets at the Feast of Tabernacles. And the subject of the present feast is the mystery of the true Feast of Tabernacles. For in it the human tabernacle is pitched by him who put on humanity for our sake. In it our tabernacles, which had fallen down through death, are fitted together again by him who built our dwelling in the beginning. Let us also speak the words of the psalm, joining the dance with David of the mighty voice: "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord." How does he come? Not as if by a ship or a carriage. He crossed over into human life through virginal incorruption. "This is our God, this is the Lord, and he has appeared to us," so that we may "establish this feast with thick boughs, up to the horns of the altar." Surely, brethren, we are not ignorant of the mystery in these words: that the whole creation is one single palace of the Lord of creation. But when sin came in, the mouths of those whom evil had seized were stopped up

and the voice of rejoicing was silenced, and the harmony of those keeping festival was torn apart, for the human creation no longer kept festival with the nature above the world. For this reason the trumpets of the prophets and apostles came. The Law calls them horns, because they are made from the true unicorn. By the power of the Spirit these sounded the word of truth intensely, so that, once the hearing of those whom sin had stopped up was opened, there might be one harmonious feast. Through the thick boughs of the Feast of Tabernacles, the lower creation would sound in concert with the powers that stand out and project around the altar above. For the horns of the spiritual altar are the projecting and prominent Powers of the intellectual nature, Principalities and Authorities, Thrones and Dominions. Human nature is joined with them in the fellowship of the feast through the Tabernacles of the resurrection, when it is covered with boughs by the renewal of bodies. For to be covered with boughs is the same as to be adorned or clothed, as those who know these things explain. Come then, let us rouse our souls to the spiritual dance and set David at the head of our choir as its leader, guide and chorus-master. With him let us speak that sweet phrase which we sang a little earlier. Let us take it up again: "This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it." On this day the darkness begins to diminish, and the measures of the night are pushed back by the growing sunlight until they vanish. It is not by some chance, brethren, that this arrangement of the feast came about of itself, so that the divine life appeared to human life at this time. Rather, through visible things creation recounts a mystery to the more discerning. It all but speaks aloud, and it teaches anyone who can hear what the lengthening day and the shortening night mean at the coming of the Lord. For I seem to hear creation saying something like this: "When you see these things, O man, understand what is hidden and is being shown to you through what is visible. Do you see how the night has advanced to its greatest length, and now halts its forward course and turns back? Understand that the evil night of sin grew as far as it could and reached, through every device of wickedness, the utmost extent of evil. Today it has been checked from spreading further, and from now on it is driven toward vanishing and destruction. Do you see the sunbeam lasting longer, and the sun higher than usual? Understand the coming of the true light, which illumines the whole world with the rays of the gospel." Perhaps, too, one might reasonably suppose the following to be the reason why the Lord did not appear at the beginning, but granted the manifestation of his divinity to human life in the last times. He who was going to mingle with human life to destroy evil necessarily waited for all [?]

the sin that the Enemy had rooted to sprout up. Only then, as the Gospel says, did he lay the axe to the root. Physicians who excel in their art act in the same way. While the fever is still smouldering inside the body and the causes of disease are gradually kindling it, they give way to the illness until the affliction reaches its crisis, and they bring the patient no help from food. But when the evil has come to a standstill and the whole disease has shown itself, then they apply their art. So too he who heals those who are sick in soul waited until the disease of evil, which had overpowered human nature, was entirely uncovered. Then nothing hidden would remain unhealed, since the physician heals only what has appeared. For this reason he did not bring the cure through his own appearing in the times of Noah, when all flesh had been corrupted in iniquity, because the shoot of Sodomite wickedness had not yet sprung up. Nor does the Lord appear at the time of the overthrow of Sodom, because many of the remaining evils still lay hidden in human nature. For where was Pharaoh, who fought against God? Where was the untamed wickedness of the Egyptians? Yet even then, I mean in the time of the Egyptians' wickedness, it was not the right moment for the Corrector of all things to mingle with life. The lawlessness of the Israelites also had to come to light. The kingdom of the Assyrians, and the pride of Nebuchadnezzar that was still smouldering in life, had to become manifest. The bloodshed against the holy ones had to shoot up like some evil, thorny growth from the wicked root of the devil. The madness of the Jews against the saints of God had to be revealed: they killed the prophets and stoned those sent to them, and at last they committed the abomination against Zechariah between the temple and the altar. Add Herod's slaughter of the children to the list of evil shoots. So the whole power of evil had been displayed from the evil root, and it had grown in many forms, running riot in the choices of those in each generation who were known for wickedness. Then, as Paul says to the Athenians, God overlooked the times of ignorance and came in the last days. It was a time when there was "none who understood and sought God," when "all had turned aside and together become worthless," when "all things were shut up under sin," when lawlessness abounded, when the gloom of evil had grown to its utmost measure. Then grace appeared, and the ray of the true light rose. Then the Sun of righteousness shone upon those who sat in darkness and the shadow of death. Then he set his foot on the dragon through human flesh, crushed its many heads, ground it into the earth and trampled it. And let no one look at the present state of life and think false what we said, that the Lord shone upon life in the last times. For an objector will perhaps say: if he waited all that time for evil to be manifested, so that he could tear it out by the roots once it had grown, he would probably have destroyed all of it, and left no remnant of it in life. But now there are murders,

and thefts [?], and adulteries, and people dare every kind of wickedness. Whoever looks at this should resolve his doubt by an example from familiar things. When snakes are killed, one can see that the trailing coil does not die at once along with the head. The head is dead, but the rest is still animated by its own fury and is not deprived of vital power. The same is true of the slayer of the dragon. When the beast had grown great, increased by every generation of men in turn, he destroyed its head, that is, the power that destroys the good, which has many heads within it. He took no account of the trailing coil, and he left the movement in the dead beast as an occasion of training for those who would come after. What then is the head that was crushed? It is the one that brought in death by its evil counsel and cast the deadly venom into man by its bite. So he who destroyed the power of death crushed the power in the serpent's head, as the Prophet says. The rest of the beast's coil, however, is scattered through human life. As long as humanity is caught up in the motions of evil, that coil keeps roughening life with the scales of sin. In power it is already dead, since the head has been made useless. But when time has passed, and all moving things come to rest at the expected end of this life, then the tail, the last thing of the Enemy, is abolished, and this is death. So the complete destruction of evil will come about, when all are called back to life through the resurrection. The righteous will be moved at once to their lot above, and those held fast by their sins will be handed over to the fire of Gehenna. But let us return to the present joy. Angels announce it to the shepherds, the heavens recount it to the Magi, and the spirit of prophecy proclaims it through many different voices, so that even the Magi became heralds of grace. For he who makes the sun rise on the just and the unjust, and sends rain on the wicked and the good, brought the ray of knowledge and the dew of the Spirit even to foreign mouths. In this way the truth would be confirmed for us all the more by the testimony of its adversaries. You hear the soothsayer Balaam, moved by a higher inspiration, prophesying among foreigners: "A star shall rise out of Jacob." You see the Magi, who traced their descent from him, watching for the rising of the new star as their forefather had foretold. Unlike the nature of the other stars, this star alone shared in both motion and rest, passing from one to the other as each was needed. Of the other stars, some are fixed once and for all in the sphere of the fixed stars and have an unmoving station, while others never cease from motion. But this one both moves, going before the Magi, and stands still, pointing out the place. You hear Isaiah crying out: "A child is born to us, and a son is given to us."

Learn from the Prophet himself how the child was born and how the son was given. Was it according to the law of nature? No, says the Prophet. The Lord of nature is not a slave to the laws of nature. But how was the child born? Tell us. "Behold," he says, "the virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel," which being interpreted is, "God with us." O the wonder! The virgin becomes a mother and remains a virgin. You see how nature is made new. With other women, as long as a woman is a virgin she is not a mother, and once she becomes a mother she no longer has her virginity. But here the two names have come together in the same person. The same woman is both mother and virgin. Her virginity did not prevent the birth, and the birth did not undo her virginity. For it was fitting that he who came into human life for the incorruption of all should begin from the incorruption of the woman who served his birth. Human usage is accustomed to call a woman who has no experience of marriage "uncorrupted." I think the great Moses foresaw this in the theophany that came to him through the light, when the fire kindled the bush and the bush did not wither. For he says, "I will cross over and see this great sight." By "crossing over" he means, I think, not motion from place to place but the passing of time. What was prefigured then in the flame and the bush was clearly revealed in the mystery of the Virgin once the intervening time had passed. As there the bush is kindled by the fire and is not burned, so here the Virgin gives birth to the light and is not corrupted. And if the bush prefigures the God-bearing body of the Virgin, do not be ashamed of the riddle. Because of its reception of sin, all flesh is sin by the very fact that it is only flesh, and Scripture calls sin by the name of thorn. If it does not carry us too far from our subject, perhaps it is not out of place to bring forward Zechariah, who was slain between the temple and the altar, as a witness to the uncorrupted mother. This Zechariah was a priest. He was not only a priest, but he also had the gift of prophecy, and the power of his prophecy is proclaimed in writing in the book of the Gospel. At that time divine grace was preparing the way, so that people would not consider a birth from a virgin incredible, and it trained the assent of the unbelieving by lesser wonders: a child is born to a barren woman past her age. This becomes the prelude to the wonder of the virgin birth. Elizabeth became a mother not by the power of nature, for she had grown old barren; the birth of the child is attributed to the divine will. In the same way, the virgin's childbirth, incredible as it seems, becomes credible when it is attributed to God. So the child of the barren woman comes before the child of the virgin. He leaped in his mother's womb at the voice of the woman who was carrying the Lord, before he himself came into the light. As soon as this forerunner of the Word was born, Zechariah's silence was loosed through prophetic

inspiration. Everything that Zechariah recounts was a prophecy of the future. The prophetic spirit led him by the hand to the knowledge of hidden things, and he understood the mystery of virginity in the incorrupt birth. So he did not exclude the unwed mother from the place in the temple that the law allotted to virgins. In this way he taught the Jews that the creator of all things and king of all creation holds human nature, along with everything else, in his hand. He leads it by his own will as he pleases and is not himself ruled by it, so it is in his power to create a new kind of birth, one that would not take virginity away from her who became a mother. For this reason he did not exclude her from the place of the virgins' choir in the temple, and this place was the space between the temple and the altar. Then they heard that the king of creation had come forth into human birth by divine dispensation. They were afraid that they would become subject to a king, so they murdered the man who bore witness to this birth, the priest who ministered at the very altar. But we have strayed far from our subject, when our discourse ought to run back to the Bethlehem of the Gospel. If we are truly shepherds and keep watch over our own flocks, the voice of the angels announcing this great joy is surely meant for us. So let us look up to the heavenly host, see the choir of angels and hear their divine hymn. What sound do those who keep the festival make? "Glory to God in the highest," they cry. Why does the voice of the angels glorify the Godhead contemplated in the highest? Because, it says, "and on earth peace" [?]. The angels have become overjoyed at what has appeared: "On earth peace." The earth that was cursed before, fertile in thorns and thistles, the place of war, the land of exile for the condemned, has received peace. O the wonder! "Truth has sprung up from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven." Such is the fruit that the earth of men has yielded. And these things happen for the sake of "good will among men." God is mingled with human nature, so that humanity may be lifted up together with the height of God. Now that we have heard these things, let us go over to Bethlehem and see the new sight: how the virgin exults in her Child, how she who knew no marriage nurses the infant. But first let us hear from those who tell her story who she is and where she came from. I have heard an apocryphal history that gives the following account of her. The Virgin's father was distinguished for his exact way of life according to the Law, and he was renowned for the finest deeds. But he was growing old without children, because his wife was not able to bear them. The Law gave a certain honour to mothers, which barren women did not share. So she followed the example of the story of Samuel's mother. She went into the Holy of Holies and became a suppliant of God. She prayed that she might not fall outside the blessing of the laws, since she had done no wrong against

the Law, but that she might become a mother and dedicate her child to God. Strengthened by the divine assent, she received the grace she had asked for. When the child was born, she named her Mary, so that the name [?] might signify the God-given character of the grace. When the girl had grown and no longer needed to cling to the breast, the mother was eager to give her back to God and fulfil her promise, and she presented [?] her in the temple. For a while the priests brought the girl up in the sanctuary, as Samuel had been brought up. But when she had grown up, they took counsel about what they should do with that holy body so as not to sin against God. To yoke her to the law of nature and make her through marriage the slave of the man who took her seemed most improper. It was thought outright sacrilege for a man to become master of an offering dedicated to God, since the laws appointed the husband to rule over his wife [?]. On the other hand, it was not lawful for a woman to live with the priests inside the sanctuary and to be seen [?] in the Holy places, and in itself it would not have been seemly [?]. While they were deliberating about this [?], counsel came from God: they should give her away under the name of betrothal, but to a man who could fittingly guard her virginity. So Joseph was found, such a man as the account required [?], of the same tribe and family as the virgin, and on the advice of the priests the girl was betrothed to him. The union went no further than betrothal. Then the virgin was initiated into the mystery by Gabriel. The words of this initiation are a blessing: "Hail," he says, "favoured one, the Lord is with you." The word now spoken to the virgin is the opposite of the word spoken to the first woman [?]. That woman was condemned to pains in childbirth because of sin, but in this one sorrow is driven out by joy. In her case pains [?] went before the birth, but here joy acts as midwife at the birth [?]. "Do not be afraid," he says. The expectation of childbirth makes every woman afraid, so the promise of a sweet childbirth drives out fear. "You will conceive," he says, "and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. For he [will save] [?] his people from their sins." What then [does Mary reply?] [?] Hear the voice of a pure virgin. The angel announces the birth, but she holds fast to her virginity [?], for she judges incorruption more precious than the angelic [announcement] [?]. She neither [disbelieves] [?] the angel, nor departs from what she has resolved. [?] "It is forbidden to me," she says. "[How will this be, since] [?] I do not know a man?" These words of Mary are proof of what was hidden. If Joseph had taken her in order to marry her, why would she have been astonished at someone announcing a birth to her? She would surely have expected to become a mother herself at some time according to the law of nature. But the flesh dedicated to God had to be kept untouched, like some holy offering. For this reason, she says, "even if you are an angel, even if you come from heaven, and [?]"

…[?] a man is what appears; but for me to know a man is out of the question. How shall I be a mother without a husband? For I know Joseph as my betrothed, but I do not know him as a husband.” What then does Gabriel, the bride's escort, say? He sets out a new bridal chamber for this pure and undefiled marriage: “The Holy Spirit,” he says, “will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.” O blessed that womb, which through its surpassing purity drew to itself the goods of the soul! For in all other cases a pure soul could scarcely receive the presence of the Holy Spirit; but here the flesh becomes a vessel of the Spirit. And then: “and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.” What does the word signify in these hidden terms? That “Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God,” as the Apostle says. So the power of the most high God, which is Christ, takes form in virginity through the coming of the Holy Spirit. For just as the shadow of bodies is shaped to the outline of the things that cast it, so the character and distinguishing marks of the Son's divinity will shine out in the power of the one being born, who is shown to be the image and seal and shadow and radiance of [?]. But the good news of the angel urges us to hasten in thought to Bethlehem and to behold the mysteries in the cave. What [?]? A child wrapped in swaddling clothes and lying in a manger; and the virgin after childbirth, the uncorrupted mother, tends her offspring. Let us, the shepherds, speak the Prophet's words: “As we have heard, so have we seen, in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God.” Did these things, then, simply happen by chance, as it fell out, and are they recorded of Christ with no meaning underlying the narrative? What does the Master's lodging in a cave mean, his lying in a manger, his being mingled with [?] at the time of the census for taxation? Is it not plain that, just as he rescues us from the curse of the law by himself becoming a curse for us, and transfers our wounds to himself so that by his wound we might be healed, so too he comes under taxation in order to free us from the evil bonds to which humanity was subject, taxed as it was by death? And when you see the cave in which the Master is born, think of the lightless, underground life of humanity, into which he comes who appears to those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death. He who takes upon himself the cords of our sins is bound tight in swaddling clothes. The manger is the dwelling of beasts without reason, and in it Reason itself, the Word, is born, so that “the ox may know its owner, and the donkey its master's manger”: the ox, yoked to the Law; the donkey, the beast of burden, laden with the sin of idolatry. Now the proper food and life of beasts without reason is grass—“He who makes grass spring up for the cattle,” says the Prophet—but the rational animal is fed on bread. For this reason, then, to the manger, which is

[St. Gregory of Nyssa] the hearth of beasts without reason, the bread of life that came down from heaven is added, so that even the creatures without reason, partaking of rational food, may come to share in Reason, the Word. So the Lord [?] stands in the manger between the ox and the donkey, so that, breaking down the dividing wall of the partition, he may create the two in himself into one new man, lifting the heavy yoke of the Law from the one and unburdening the other of the load of idolatry. But let us look up at the wonders of heaven. For see, not only prophets and angels announce this joy to us; the heavens too proclaim the glory of the Gospel through their own wonders. Christ has risen for us out of Judah, as the Apostle says, yet the Jew is not illumined by the one who has risen. The Magi are strangers to the covenants of promise and aliens to the blessing of the Fathers; yet they outstrip the people of Israel in knowledge, recognizing the heavenly luminary and not failing to know the King in the cave. They bring gifts; these plot. They worship; these persecute. They rejoice at finding the one they sought; these are troubled at the birth of the one announced. For, it says, “when the Magi saw the star over the place where the child was, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy.” “But when Herod heard the word, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him.” The former offer frankincense to him as to God, and honor his royal dignity with gold; and by a kind of prophetic grace they signify through the myrrh the dispensation of his Passion. The latter decree the utter destruction of all the young. This, it seems to me, convicts them not only of bitterness but of the utmost folly. For what did the slaughter of children mean to them? And to what end did these murderers dare such an abomination? “Because,” it says, “a new sign among the wonders of heaven announced to the Magi the manifestation of the King.” What then? Do you believe the sign that announced it to be true, or do you suspect the rumor to be empty? If he is such as to dispose the heavens in accord with himself, he is surely beyond the reach of your hand. But if his living or dying depends on you, you fear such a one in vain. For one so placed as to be subject to your power—why is he plotted against? Why is that dreadful command sent out? O wicked sentence against the infants, that the wretched [?] should be slain! What wrong had they done? What cause for death and punishment had they furnished against themselves? They had only one charge against them: that they had been born and come into the light. And for this the city had to be filled with executioners, and a throng of mothers and infants gathered, with crowds standing by them, and the parents, and, as is likely, all their kinsfolk flocking to the tragedy. Who could depict these calamities in words? Who could bring the sufferings before the eyes by narration? That mingled lament? That mournful chorus

of children, mothers, relatives, fathers, crying out piteously against the threats of the executioners? How could anyone describe the executioner standing over the infant with his naked sword, glaring fiercely and murderously and uttering other such things, dragging the baby toward himself with one hand and raising the sword with the other; and the mother on the other side pulling the child back toward herself and putting her own neck beneath the sword's edge, so that she might not see with her own eyes her poor little child destroyed by the executioner's hands? How could anyone recount what the fathers suffered: the cries of recall, the wailing, the last embraces of their children—and many such things happening at once in the same place? Who could set forth as tragedy the manifold and varied calamity, the double birth-pangs of women newly delivered, the fierce burning of nature? How the wretched infant clung to the breast and at the same moment received the mortal blow through its vitals? How the wretched mother both held the nipple to the infant's mouth and received her child's blood in her bosom? Often, no doubt, the executioner, by the force of his arm, drove through child and mother together with a single thrust of the sword, and the stream of blood became one, mingled from the mother's wound and the child's fatal blow. And since this too is added to Herod's foul command—that the death sentence was issued not only against the newborn, but that anyone who had reached his second year should also be seized (for it is written, “from two years old and under”)—the account sees here, as is likely, yet another suffering: that the interval had often made the same woman the mother of two children. What a sight, then, there was again in such cases: two executioners busy about one mother, one dragging toward himself the child running at her side, the other tearing the nursling from her bosom! What must the wretched mother have suffered at this, her nature split between two children, each equally kindling fire in her maternal heart, not knowing which of the wicked executioners to follow, as they dragged the infants off to slaughter, one this way and the other that? Should she run to the newborn, still uttering an indistinct and inarticulate wail? But she hears the other, who can already speak, calling his mother with lisping voice and tears. What is she to do? What is to become of her? Whose cry will she answer? Whose wailing will she echo with her own? Which death will she lament, scourged perhaps by the goads of nature over each of them? But let us turn our hearing away from the laments over the children, and direct our minds to things more cheerful and more fitting to the feast, even though, as the prophecy says, Rachel cries aloud lamenting the slaughter of her children. For “on a feast day,” as the wise Solomon says, “forgetfulness of evils is fitting.” And what feast could be more auspicious for us than this one, on which the Sun of righteousness, scattering the evil darkness of the devil, shines upon our nature through our very nature; on which what had fallen

is raised up, what was at war is brought to reconciliation, what was cast out is brought back, what had fallen from life returns to life, what was enslaved in captivity is restored to royal dignity, and what was fettered by the bonds of death runs back free to the land of the living? Now, according to the prophecy, the bronze gates of Death are shattered; the iron bars are broken by which the human race was formerly shut up in the prison of death. Now, as David says, the gate of righteousness is opened. Now the sound of those keeping the feast is heard in one voice throughout the whole world. Through a man came death, and through a man salvation. The first fell into sin; the second raised up the fallen. Woman has been vindicated by woman: the first gave sin its entry, but this one served the entry of righteousness. That one took in the serpent's counsel; this one brought forth the slayer of the serpent and gave birth to the author of light. That one brought in sin through the tree; this one brought in the good in its place through the tree. By tree I mean the cross; and the fruit of this tree becomes ever-blooming and unfading life for those who taste it. And let no one suppose that such thanksgiving befits the mystery of Pascha alone. Let him consider that Pascha is the completion of the dispensation. How could there have been the completion unless the beginning had led the way? Which of the two comes first? Plainly the birth, in the dispensation that culminated in the Passion. Therefore the goods of Pascha too are part of the praises of the Nativity. And if one lists the benefits recorded in the Gospels and recounts the miracles of healing—the food produced from nothing, the return of the dead from their tombs, the impromptu cultivation of wine, the flight of demons, the change of every kind of suffering into health, the leaping of the lame, the eyes made of clay, the divine teachings, the laws, the initiation into higher things through parables—all these are the grace of this present day, for it began the goods that followed. Therefore “let us rejoice and be glad in it,” not fearing the reproach of men nor being overcome by their contempt, as the prophet too urges—those who mock the account of the dispensation, as though it were unseemly for the Lord to enter the nature of a body and to mingle himself with human life through birth, not knowing, it seems, the mystery of this, how the wisdom of God arranged our salvation. Willingly we sold ourselves to our sins; like slaves bought with silver we were enslaved to the enemy of our life. What would you most have wished to receive from the Master? Was it not to be rescued from your calamity? Why do you pry into the manner of it? Why do you lay down laws for your benefactor while failing to lay hold of the benefit? It is as if someone were to push the doctor away and find fault with his kindness because he applied the

treatment not in this way but in another. But if out of curiosity you inquire into the magnitude of the dispensation, it is enough for you to learn this much: that the Divine is not some single good only, but whatever can be conceived as good, that it is—powerful, just, good, wise, all the names and notions that signify what befits God. Consider, then, whether all the qualities mentioned did not concur in what was done for us: goodness, wisdom, power, justice. As good, he loved the apostate; as wise, he devised the means of return for those who had been enslaved; as just, he does not use force against the enslaver, who had acquired them justly by purchase, but gave himself as a ransom in exchange for those held captive, so that, like a guarantor who takes the debt upon himself, he might free [?] the one held captive. As powerful, he was not held fast by Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption. For it was not possible for the author of life to be held by corruption. But is it shameful to enter human birth and to undergo the experience of the sufferings of the flesh? What you are describing is the surpassing greatness of the benefit. For since humanity could not otherwise be rescued from such great evils, the King of all impassibility consented to exchange his own glory for our life. And purity comes into our filth, but the filth does not cling to the purity, as the Gospel says: “The light shone in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it.” For the gloom vanishes at the presence of the ray; the sun is not dimmed by the gloom. What is mortal is swallowed up by life, as the Apostle says; life is not consumed by death. What was corrupted is saved together with the incorruptible; corruption does not cling to incorruption. For this reason a common chorus of all creation arises, all sending up a single song of praise to the Master of creation, every tongue of things in heaven and on earth and under the earth crying out that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father, blessed to the ages of ages. Amen.
